content: The Bouba/Kiki Effect was first identified in 1929 by Wolfgang Köhler, a German-American psychologist. During his experiments on the island of Tenerife, Köhler presented participants with two distinct shapes: one jagged and angular, and the other smooth and rounded. He observed that participants consistently associated the jagged shape with the word takete and the rounded shape with the word baluba (later changed to maluma in a 1947 version of the study). In 2001, researchers Vilayanur S. Ramachandran and Edward Hubbard revisited Köhler's experiment, this time using the words kiki and bouba. They asked participants, Which of these shapes is bouba, and which is kiki? Across a large sample of English and Tamil speakers, 95% to 98% of participants identified the rounded shape as bouba and the jagged shape as kiki. This finding suggests that the human brain has an inherent ability to extract abstract properties from both visual shapes and auditory sounds. Interestingly, even young children who are not yet able to read exhibit this effect, indicating that it is not dependent on literacy or language proficiency. Ramachandran and Hubbard proposed that the Bouba/Kiki Effect has significant implications for the evolution of language. Specifically, it challenges the notion that the naming of objects is entirely arbitrary. For example, the word bouba may be associated with the rounded shape because the act of producing the b sound involves a rounded mouth shape, whereas the production of the k sound in kiki requires a more angular and taut mouth movement. Additionally, the k sound is sharper and more forceful compared to the softer b sound. The researchers also suggested that this phenomenon might represent a neurological basis for sound symbolism, where sounds are non-arbitrarily linked to objects and events in the world. This synesthesia-like mapping between sounds and shapes could provide insight into how humans perceive and categorize sensory information. Interestingly, individuals with autism do not exhibit the Bouba/Kiki Effect to the same extent as neurotypical individuals. While the general population agrees with the typical associations about 90% of the time, individuals with autism only agree approximately 60% of the time. This difference may provide further insight into the neurological and cognitive mechanisms underlying this phenomenon.
